claims_disputed.claim: GPT-5.4 (Codex) and Opus 4.7 (Claude Code) lead at 43.49±3.32 and 41.89±3.31 Pass@1; the best open-weight model GLM 5 scores 24.03
claims_disputed.reason: Table 1 computes Wilson 95% CIs 'at the trial level', treating the three trials of each task as independent samples, so the intervals ignore task clustering and are too narrow. All of Q&A, and the must-have rubric half of Test Writing and Refactoring, is graded by one Anthropic judge (Opus 4.5, App. J) with no same-family bias check, while three of the top five configurations are Claude models. The frontier vs open-weight gap of about 18 points survives these caveats, but the precise numbers and intervals as stated do not merit 'strong'.

claims_disputed.claim: Top models rely on extensive codebase exploration and runtime-driven reasoning
claims_disputed.reason: The only quantitative support is a cross-model scatter of Pass@1 against mean code executions for 8 models (Fig. 3a), where stronger models also differ in every other respect, plus anecdotes. No run removes or adds execution for a fixed model. The '46% No Runtime Evidence' breakdown (Fig. 3b) is an unvalidated Opus 4.6 classification. 'Rely on' is a causal claim the design cannot support.

pattern_stance_changes.reason: The review itself says QA agents 'are not compared with docs, static-only reading, or human onboarding'. With no isolating comparison, a capability ceiling (Q&A Pass@1 about 41%, Table 1) is 'introduces', not 'mixed'. The only within-model comparison on Q&A is native scaffold vs mini-SWE-agent (40.8 vs 36.3 for GPT-5.4, 40.3 vs 36.0 for Opus 4.7), which concerns the harness, not whether a QA agent beats an alternative way of answering.

missed_issues: Agents had internet access throughout (Harbor requirement, App. I). The solution-lookup audit covers only 210 trials and does not say which subset; 4 lookups were found. The authors themselves say future runs should disable internet.

The human-LLM agreement set (Table 5) is 200 rubric items pooled across all three workflows, graded on Opus 4.5 and GPT-5 outputs. The paper does not say who the human graders were or give per-workflow agreement. Q&A, the track most relevant to onboarding, has no programmatic check at all, so it is the one most exposed to judge error.

The Test Writing mutation check is one hand-authored whole-function no-op stub per task (App. D). It catches assertion-free tests but not subtle regressions, which the authors concede ('coarse necessary signal').

The native-vs-minimal scaffold comparison is uneven across vendors: Harbor's Codex CLI had no subagent dispatch at the time (§4.5), so 'native scaffold' means different feature sets for OpenAI and Anthropic models.
'As models improve, they write fewer, more precise tests' (§4.3, Fig. 4b) is another between-model association presented as a trend.

The full authoring manual is withheld as proprietary (App. D), so task construction cannot be reproduced even though tasks and graders are released. App. B traces only the Anthropic Opus family over time, on a 30-task subset.
note: I agree this is a careful benchmark with three trials, a human-checked rubric judge and released tasks. Its Q&A track is directly relevant to onboarding, and its refactor and test-writing gaps are useful. I would not admit it without caveats: the paper's own judge, from the same model family as half the leaderboard, grades the paper's own tasks, and the CIs ignore task clustering, so I lower the headline numbers to moderate. The exploration and runtime-reasoning story is a between-model correlation and should be weak. On patterns, P43 has no comparison against any alternative, so it is 'introduces'. I keep P18 as 'supports' because judge-human agreement is reported and high.
